title: Hanyang: Capital Relocation, Urban Planning, and Sacred Geography
description: Hanyang reveals how a dynasty turned landscape into government and government into urban space.

blocks.title: Choosing a political center
paragraphs: A new dynasty needed a place from which to govern, but a capital was far more than a convenient headquarters. It housed officials, ritual sites, stores, workshops, military facilities, markets, and the residences of people whose labor sustained the court. Choosing a city meant imagining how a new political order should appear in space. Early Joseon’s move toward Hanyang was therefore an act of state-making as well as urban planning.

The location offered geographical advantages, yet the arguments for it also drew upon ideas about auspicious setting, defensibility, access, and centrality. It is tempting to read later city growth backward and treat the eventual capital as the only possible choice. At the time, alternatives and disagreements formed part of the process.

blocks.title: Palace, gates, and streets
paragraphs: A planned royal capital makes power visible. The position of gates, major roads, palace compounds, state offices, and ritual buildings tells people where authority is located and how it expects the city to function. Such arrangements are not merely aesthetic. They affect movement, access to officials, patterns of commerce, and the daily journeys of workers who keep a city operating.

The ideal city described in planning language could never perfectly predict the city people actually inhabited. Population changes, household needs, fires, repairs, and commerce continually altered the built environment. The physical capital was both a political statement and a changing urban organism.

blocks.title: Work behind the royal city
paragraphs: Palaces do not construct themselves. Building and maintaining an urban center required timber, stone, transport, food supply, skilled craftspeople, and large numbers of laborers. These needs connected the new capital to the countryside and to river routes. A capital concentrates resources, making its apparent grandeur inseparable from the wider economy that sustains it.

Markets and neighborhoods grew within an administrative landscape. A person working as a merchant, porter, craftsperson, or servant encountered the royal city from a very different angle than a court official entering an audience hall. Both experiences belong in the history of Hanyang.

blocks.title: The afterlife of a foundation
paragraphs: Over time, the city became layered with memories of reform, conflict, occupation, modernization, and growth. Later Seoul cannot simply be equated with early Joseon Hanyang, but its historical geography provides a powerful way to trace continuities and ruptures. Streets and landmarks carry names whose meanings shift across centuries.

Studying the founding capital opens routes into architecture, ritual government, rivers and transport, urban everyday life, and the changing political geography of Korea. The story is not only that a ruler chose a city; it is that generations of people continuously remade it.
